entityDossier.whatItIs: An external scientific advisory body stood up in June 2026 at the request of the White House and in coordination with AARO, ODNI, the FBI and the wider Intelligence Community, chaired by Harvard astrophysicist Abraham (Avi) Loeb. It reports to a higher-level interagency UAP Governance Board co-established by ODNI, the FBI and the Department of War, which held its first meeting on 16 June 2026. Every dataset the council is given is unclassified by design.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: The council is the scientific-legitimacy layer bolted onto the 2026 disclosure architecture, and its terms of reference are the tell. It exists to advise on the coordinated declassification of UAP information under Executive Order 13526, yet its own members are restricted to unclassified data — a body chartered to resolve the mystery is structurally barred from the evidence that would resolve it. Its membership includes Rear Admiral (ret.) Tim Gallaudet, whose account of a 2015 SIPRNET email titled "Urgent safety of flight issue" being deleted overnight from a flag officer's classified system is one of the most concrete public allegations of a special access program reaching into fleet communications; and Prof. Garry Nolan, whose laboratory work on claimed anomalous materials is the closest civilian science has come to the custody question. The council therefore places people with direct knowledge of concealment inside the advisory apparatus while denying them access to the compartments. Loeb's own public framing — that the "down-to-Earth interpretation" is adversary technology and compromised espionage defence — supplies the administration with an alarm-raising narrative that never touches the legacy retrieval question.
entityDossier.narrative:
On 16 June 2026, Avi Loeb published a Medium post announcing that he had been "tasked by the White House, the Pentagon's All Domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO), the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), the FBI, and the Intelligence Community, to assemble a 'UAP Science Advisory Council'." The following day DefenseScoop's Brandi Vincent confirmed the arrangement with an ODNI official, who described the parent UAP Governance Board as an interagency body created "to provide guidance, recommendations and coordination at the interagency level, bringing together military, law enforcement, the intelligence community, and other civilian agencies," and confirmed that it had met for the first time the previous day. The ODNI official declined to identify the board's original participants — the body that will control declassification sequencing is itself anonymous.

The council's composition is the most analytically useful fact about it, and the two authoritative lists do not match. Loeb's own 16 June account names fifteen members: Prof. Liberty Vittert Capito (data analysis and statistics), Prof. Carol Cleland (anomaly identification), Dr. Richard Cloete (data analysis and AI tools), Dr. Omer Eldadi (data management, AI, human psychology), Dr. Tim Gallaudet (oceanography), Prof. Robin Hanson (statistics and economics), Ross Howard (communication), Dr. Kevin Knuth (physics and instrumentation), Ben Lamm (oceanography and biology), Dr. Devesh Nandal (numerical analysis and astrophysics), Prof. Garry Nolan (molecular biology and materials science), Dr. Michael Shermer (the study of anomalies), Dr. Peter Skafish (anthropology), Prof. Matthew Szydagis (instrumentation and data collection), and Dr. Jennice Vilhauer (quantitative psychology). The list Loeb supplied to DefenseScoop one day later drops Vittert Capito, Hanson and Knuth — three of the four quantitative-methods seats — and is otherwise identical. Whether that is editorial compression or a roster in flux within twenty-four hours is unresolved, but it is a documented discrepancy between two dated statements by the same source.

Loeb is explicit about the design intent behind Shermer's inclusion: "Including at least one member with a skeptical perspective (or a designated 'devil's advocate') in every committee is highly important. The skeptic prevents blind spots, reduces cognitive biases, and actively protects groups from disastrous decision-making as a result of groupthink." Read against the stance of this board, a council that pre-installs its own debunker and pre-commits to unclassified-only inputs has been engineered for a specific class of output: methodological recommendations, sensor procurement advice, and the repeated observation that better data is needed. It cannot produce a finding about custody, because it will never see a custody record.

The council's first substantive engagement with government product illustrates the boundary. Loeb pointed to an AARO report dated 5 June 2026, signed by AARO Director Dr. Jon Kosloski and posted in the third PURSUE tranche as DOW-UAP-D077, "Unresolved Case Analysis Update — Western United States Event." Loeb's summary: during two days in October 2023, law enforcement officials observed anomalous phenomena including an orange "mother" orb launching smaller red orbs, and about 40 percent of the reported phenomena lack a reasonable explanation and remain unresolved. That is the council's raw material — a published, unresolved case file, offered to outside scientists after AARO has already declined to resolve it.

The personnel overlaps are where the network becomes legible. Gallaudet is the former Oceanographer of the Navy, former commander of Naval Meteorology and Oceanography Command, and former Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Oceans and Atmosphere. He is also an advisor to Ryan Graves's Americans for Safe Aerospace, and it was through Graves's sworn July 2023 testimony that his account of the deleted Fleet Forces Command email entered the congressional record. The man whose story is the strongest public evidence that a special access program suppressed a safety-of-flight warning about the very encounters that produced the GO FAST video now sits on the government's own science council — advising on declassification, with unclassified data only.

Loeb's institutional history matters too. He served on the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST) in 2019-2020, chaired Harvard's Astronomy department 2011-2020, chaired the National Academies' Board on Physics and Astronomy 2018-2021, and has run the Galileo Project since roughly 2021, which now operates three observatories scanning for objects outside the performance envelope of human technology. He is, in short, exactly the kind of credentialed outsider whose participation converts a political disclosure exercise into something that reads as science — and whose access constraints guarantee it will remain an exercise. The sequencing underlines the point: three PURSUE tranches had already gone public before the council was constituted, so the scientific advisory body was assembled after the declassification pipeline was already running.

entityDossier.whatItIs: An Office of the Director of National Intelligence memorandum titled "Preliminary Guidance for Implementation of NDA Waiver," bearing control number ES 2026-00818, dated 31 July 2026, from the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence to the Director of the Central Intelligence Agency and other IC element heads. It directs the Department of War and the Intelligence Community to build a process by which current and former employees and contractors may disclose UAP information to AARO or to designated representatives of the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE) Task Force notwithstanding existing non-disclosure agreements, agreements, oaths or commitments.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: The memo is an admission written in the form of a remedy. No government waives non-disclosure obligations for a subject about which nothing is being withheld. Its most consequential sentence is the one instructing the IC to make its workforce aware that any NDA prohibiting disclosure to the President, the PURSUE Task Force or other designees is no longer in force — an instruction that only makes sense if such instruments exist, and DLA Piper's government contracts practice notes that an NDA barring disclosure to the President "would be unusual if not unlawful" because the President is the ultimate classification authority. It was not published by ODNI. The administration authorised the House office of Rep. Eric Burlison, a founding member of the Congressional UAP Caucus, to distribute it — routing an IC-wide directive through the oversight bloc rather than dni.gov. And it is materially narrower than the statute it purports to implement: 50 U.S.C. § 3373b already authorises disclosure to AARO notwithstanding Executive Order 13526, the Atomic Energy Act, and Section 798 of the Espionage Act, while the memo reaches only contractual and oath-based restrictions.
entityDossier.narrative:
On 31 July 2026 the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence signed a memorandum, numbered ES 2026-00818, addressed to the Director of the CIA and the heads of the other Intelligence Community elements. Two days later Rep. Eric Burlison (MO-07) posted it on his House website, noting that "the administration authorized Congressman Burlison's office to publicly distribute the memorandum." That single procedural fact deserves more attention than the memo's contents. The executive branch chose, as the public release channel for a national-level intelligence directive, the congressional office of a member who had spent three years accusing the executive branch of hiding UAP records — and who ten days earlier, on 21 July 2026, had publicly invited anyone who believed the President's directive applied to them to contact his office for help navigating the process. Burlison's office was, in effect, standing up a parallel intake channel for whistleblowers while the official one was still being written.

What the memo does: it directs the Department of War and the IC to implement a process ensuring that current and former governmental employees and contractors holding alleged UAP information may disclose it to designated government representatives in AARO or the PURSUE Task Force notwithstanding contravening NDAs, agreements, oaths or commitments. It instructs every IC element, within thirty days of receipt, to coordinate with ODNI to establish a PURSUE designee and to "inform their workforce of the President's order." It states that NDAs prohibiting disclosure to the President, to PURSUE or to other designees are no longer in force. And it flags two further tranches of guidance to come — implementing guidance for the preliminary guidance itself, and a separate ODNI/DoW package for the broader PURSUE transparency project.

What the memo does not do is the more informative half. It does not authorise public disclosure of classified information. It does not authorise disclosure to Congress other than through AARO or existing channels — a striking limitation given that the standard ODNI classified information nondisclosure agreement, Standard Form 312, already contemplates disclosure to Congress in some form. It does not tell government contractors, as distinct from IC employees, how to make an authorised disclosure at all, even though the FY2023 NDAA's anti-retaliation protection expressly extends to any "contractor, subcontractor, grantee, subgrantee, or personal services contractor" of a covered department or agency. For an entity board built on the premise that the retrieval and reverse-engineering work sits inside cleared private industry, that omission is the operative fact: the memo waives the secrecy instruments of the government workforce while leaving the contractor workforce — the population most likely to hold the material — without a documented route.

The memo is also narrower than the law. Section 1673 of the FY2023 NDAA (Pub. L. No. 117-263, 136 Stat. 2959-62, codified at 50 U.S.C. § 3373b(b)(1)) authorises disclosure to AARO notwithstanding not merely NDAs but any regulation or order issued under Executive Order 13526, anything under the Atomic Energy Act, Section 798 of the Espionage Act, and any other "provision of law relating to the disclosure of information." ES 2026-00818 speaks only to "[NDAs], agreements, oaths, or commitments." As agency guidance it is not binding law, and DLA Piper's alert notes that it "does not, by itself, confer legal rights with respect to making authorized disclosures beyond those established by statute." A person weighing whether to come forward is therefore being handed a document that sounds like permission and is legally less protective than the statute already on the books — and told that the real guidance is still being drafted. That is a structure that produces delay.

The scale problem is visible in AARO's own reporting. Its Fiscal Year 2025 Consolidated Annual Report states that between 2 June 2024 and 30 May 2025, seven individuals contacted AARO with UAP-related claims that AARO judged warranted a request for a follow-on interview. Seven. The same report asserts that AARO is legally authorised to receive all UAP-related information at any level of classification regardless of restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented access programs. Those two statements coexisting is the concealment argument in miniature: an office with unlimited statutory reach and a single-digit annual intake.

Context matters for dating. The PURSUE Task Force was launched by the Department of War on 1 May 2026 following President Trump's 19 February 2026 Truth Social directive; the first tranche of records went public on 8 May 2026, with further tranches on 22 May, 12 June, 10 July and 7 August 2026. ES 2026-00818 arrives at the end of that sequence, nearly three months into a rolling public release — the NDA waiver follows the file dumps rather than preceding them, which means the population best able to contextualise those files was still under contractual gag while the files were being published.

One further structural note. AARO sits inside the Department of War but reports to ODNI on operational and security matters under 50 U.S.C. § 3373(b)(3)(B)(ii). ES 2026-00818 was issued by ODNI, while the FY2023 NDAA assigns the establishment of the secure disclosure mechanism to the Secretary of War acting through the head of AARO in consultation with the DNI. The guidance therefore comes from the consulted party rather than the responsible one — a jurisdictional wrinkle that any contractor's counsel will find, and that gives every recipient a colourable argument that the instrument binding them has not yet been properly issued.

entityDossier.whatItIs: A set of 38 Defense Intelligence Reference Documents (DIRDs) produced between roughly 2008 and 2010 as deliverables of the Defense Intelligence Agency's Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP), later known as the Advanced Aviation Threat Identification Program (AATIP), contracted to Robert Bigelow's Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS). The titles and authors were compiled by DIA at the request of the offices of Senators John McCain and Jack Reed and released to the Federation of American Scientists under FOIA on 16 January 2019; 37 of the 38 documents themselves were released by DIA under FOIA in 2022.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: The DIRD list is the closest thing in the public record to a published requirements document for a reverse-engineering effort. A conventional foreign-threat forecasting portfolio does not commission papers on traversable wormholes, stargates and negative energy, warp drive and the manipulation of extra dimensions, invisibility cloaking, antigravity for aerospace applications and metamaterials. That is a menu of observed capabilities in search of a physics, written by a tight network around Bigelow — Hal Puthoff and Eric Davis of EarthTech International, Kit Green, George Hathaway, Paul Czysz — and paid for out of a roughly $22 million defense intelligence line between 2008 and 2012. DIA's own framing in the cover letter to the Senate Armed Services Committee, that "the purpose of AATIP was to investigate foreign advanced aerospace weapons threats from the present out to the next 40 years," is itself the artifact of concealment: it recasts stargates as threat forecasting. The classification pattern reinforces it. Thirty-seven of the 38 carry only "For Official Use Only"; exactly one was produced in two versions, the second classified Secret with a foreign-national release restriction. A single deliverable set with a two-tier publication scheme is where the applied work hides.
entityDossier.narrative:
The DIRDs exist in the public record because two Senate offices asked a question. DIA compiled the list of every product produced under the AATIP contract at the request of the offices of Senator John McCain, then Chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, and Senator Jack Reed, its ranking Democrat. Steven Aftergood of the Federation of American Scientists' Project on Government Secrecy obtained the five-page document under FOIA on 16 January 2019, and Nick Pope obtained the same package the same month; George Knapp's I-Team at Las Vegas CBS affiliate KLAS had already published a near-complete list of titles and authors in July 2018. The cover letter's operative sentence reads: "Based on interest from your staff regarding the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA)'s role in the Advanced Aviation Threat Identification Program (AATIP) please find attached a list of all products produced under the AATIP contract for DIA to publish."

The program's origin is documented but blurred by three names for one thing. It began in 2007 as the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications program (AAWSA/AAWSAP), was contracted to BAASS under a DIA solicitation, and came to be known publicly as AATIP after December 2017. DIA spent approximately $22 million between 2008 and 2012 and produced 38 reports. The technical papers commissioned by BAASS were converted into Defense Intelligence Reference Documents by DIA's James T. Lacatski — the individual who is also, by his own later account, the government official who conceived and championed the program. AATIP sat inside DIA's Defense Warning Office, a unit created in 2002 to monitor threats to U.S. interests in critical regions, which is the bureaucratic camouflage: an office whose remit is strategic surprise is exactly where you park a program about technologies nobody can explain.

The authorship concentration is the analytically load-bearing fact. Puthoff and Davis of EarthTech International in Austin, Texas were primary authors on six of the 38 between them, and Davis is a co-author on a seventh from independent consultant Richard Obousy. Because the DIA list records only the primary author, the true EarthTech footprint is unknowable from the document. Both men have prior ties to Bigelow's National Institute for Discovery Science (NIDSci). Puthoff went on to To The Stars Academy alongside Luis Elizondo, the DoD official who publicly identified himself as running AATIP — meaning the research network, the government program office and the 2017 disclosure vehicle share personnel across all three layers. Other named contributors are more conventional: Ulf Leonhardt of the University of St Andrews wrote "Invisibility Cloaking" and is a genuine authority on transformation optics; Lockheed Martin supplied three reports including one on fusion power and one titled "Air Breathing Propulsion and Power for Aerospace Applications"; Directed Technologies, Inc. of Virginia supplied the high energy laser weapon work. More than half of the 38 came from authors at academic institutions including UNLV, the University of Nevada-Reno, Ohio State and St Andrews. Marc Millis, the former NASA propulsion engineer who founded the Tau Zero Foundation, is among the authors — a direct thread between the DIRD collection and NASA's institutional periphery.

One procurement decision inside the set is indefensible on its face and therefore diagnostic. Robert Baker's company GravWave supplied a report on high-frequency gravitational waves. In 2008 the JASON advisory group had reviewed separate HFGW work Baker had done for the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and concluded: "The proposed applications of the science of HFGW are fundamentally wrong" and "No foreign threat in HFGW is credible." DIA funded the topic anyway. Either the program office did not read the JASON review — implausible for a defense intelligence element — or topic selection was driven by something other than technical merit review. The second possibility is the interesting one: a portfolio assembled to cover a hypothesis space rather than to assess adversary capability.

The classification arithmetic completes the picture. entityDossier.whatItIs: The sustained series of unidentified object encounters reported by U.S. Navy aircrews operating with Carrier Air Wing One and the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group off the U.S. East Coast from roughly the summer of 2014 through the Roosevelt's 2015 deployment work-ups. The episode produced the two ATFLIR infrared videos known publicly as GIMBAL and GOFAST, both of which the Navy has officially dated to 21 January 2015.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: This is the case in which a U.S. Navy fighter squadron documented an unidentified object corridor over an active training range for months, and the institutional response was to erase the paperwork rather than identify the objects. Ryan Graves testified under oath that after a near-collision at the W-72 entry point his squadron submitted a safety report and there was "no official acknowledgement of the incident and no further mechanism to report the sightings." The stronger allegation, entered into the same congressional record, comes from Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet: a 2015 SIPRNET email from the Fleet Forces operations commander to all one- and two-star admirals, titled "Urgent safety of flight issue" and attaching the GO FAST video, was removed from his and his deputy's classified systems the next day and never discussed — which he attributes to a classified special access program. That is a documented instance of a compartmented program reaching into a flag officer's classified mail to delete a safety-of-flight warning. Meanwhile the Navy's own on-record position is that it "considers the phenomena contained/depicted in those 3 videos as unidentified" and will provide "no details on individual reports."
entityDossier.narrative:
In 2014, Lieutenant Ryan Graves was flying F/A-18F Super Hornets with Strike Fighter Squadron 11 out of the Virginia Beach area. Following an upgrade to the squadron's radar, aircrews began detecting unknown objects in their operating airspace. The tracks were initially dismissed as software glitches until they were corroborated with infrared sensors, at which point, in Graves's words, the sightings "became an open secret among our aircrew" and "were so frequent that they became part of daily briefs."

The pivotal incident occurred in Warning Area W-72, a block of restricted airspace ten miles east of Virginia Beach through which all traffic enters at a single GPS point and set altitude. Graves testified: "Just at the moment the two jets crossed the threshold, one of the pilots saw a dark gray cube inside of a clear sphere — motionless against the wind, fixed directly at the entry point. The jets, only 100 feet apart, were forced to take evasive action. They terminated the mission immediately and returned to base. Our squadron submitted a safety report, but there was no official acknowledgement of the incident and no further mechanism to report the sightings." His description of the objects' performance is specific and falsifiable: they "could accelerate at speeds up to Mach 1, hold their position against hurricane-force winds, and outlast our fighter jets, operating continuously throughout the day," with "no visible means of lift, control surfaces or propulsion."

The cover-up allegation is Gallaudet's, and Graves put it in the record. While serving as an admiral at Fleet Forces Command, Gallaudet received a classified SIPRNET email in 2015 from his boss, the Operations Commander, addressed to all one- and two-star admiral subordinates. The subject line was "Urgent safety of flight issue." Attached was the GO FAST video from a Navy F/A-18. The email asked whether anyone knew the objects' origin, expressed concern about multiple near mid-air collisions with UAP in the early warning area off Virginia Beach — the same airspace as Graves's encounters — and raised the possibility of shutting down the exercise for safety reasons. Gallaudet reviewed it with his deputy. The next day the email was gone from both their systems. Despite routine in-person meetings of that same group, no one ever discussed it. Gallaudet presumes it was removed in connection with a classified special access program, and has stated publicly that after seeing the report he did not believe the objects represented any known human technology.

The Navy's public position is a study in minimal concession. In September 2019, Joseph Gradisher, official spokesperson for the Deputy Chief of Naval Operations for Information Warfare, told The Black Vault that the Navy's official identifiers for the videos do not match the TTSA names FLIR1, Gimbal and GoFast — the Navy identifies them by the dates of the observations — and then supplied the dates: "[The] dates are 14 November 2004 for 'FLIR1' and 21 January 2015 for both 'Gimbal' and 'GoFast.'" That single sentence established for the first time that GIMBAL and GOFAST were recorded on the same day and may be two aspects of a single event. Gradisher went on: "The Navy has not publicly released characterizations or descriptions, nor released any hypothesis or conclusions, in regard to the objects contained in the referenced videos," while conceding that "The Navy considers the phenomena contained/depicted in those 3 videos as unidentified." Asked for the location, the answer was: "We will not be providing any details on individual reports." The Navy also confirmed the footage had never been cleared for public release when To The Stars Academy published it in December 2017 and March 2018.

Geography can be reconstructed anyway. Filmmaker Dave Beaty worked the deck logs of USS Normandy, the cruiser escorting the Roosevelt, and placed her on 21 January 2015 slightly more than 100 miles east, roughly equidistant between Jacksonville and Savannah — the JAX operating area. A cruiser stays with the carrier during operations, so the deck log fixes the approximate position of the encounter that the Navy declined to disclose.

What happened afterward is the concealment argument's second half. Graves testified that "all UAP videos since 2021 are classified Secret or above, which prevents the American people and even some Members of Congress from seeing UAP videos like the full GIMBAL video recorded by my squadron." The 2021 UAP Task Force preliminary assessment reported eleven near misses with UAP; Graves said he understood the number had grown. In April 2022 the FAA issued an alert to its operations managers that a commercial aircraft over West Virginia had experienced a double attitude and double autopilot failure while flying under a UAP. Graves founded Americans for Safe Aerospace, which by July 2023 had nearly 5,000 members and was working with more than 30 UAP witnesses, most of whom refuse to speak publicly for fear of professional consequences; he also chairs the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics' UAP Integration and Outreach Committee with roughly 80 volunteer PhDs and aerospace engineers. In his testimony he noted that among the accounts reaching ASA, "in several, sensor data was escalated for analysis and there were profound irregularities in how the data was handled" — the same signature as the deleted email, reported independently by other witnesses.

The loop closes in June 2026. Gallaudet — the flag officer whose deleted email is the strongest public evidence that a special access program suppressed a UAP safety warning about this exact airspace — was named to the government's new UAP Science Advisory Council, seated for oceanography, and restricted to unclassified data.

entityDossier.whatItIs: A bipartisan House caucus launched by Rep. Tim Burchett (TN-02) in August 2023 and co-chaired with Rep. Jared Moskowitz (FL-23). Its founding cohort — the six members who signed its first act, a letter to the Inspector General of the Intelligence Community — were Burchett, Moskowitz, Anna Paulina Luna (FL-13), Nancy Mace (SC-01), Eric Burlison (MO-07) and Andy Ogles (TN-05).
entityDossier.whyImplicated: The caucus is the only organised bloc in Congress whose founding premise is that UAP crash retrieval and reverse-engineering programs exist and have been concealed from the committees of jurisdiction. Its very first act, less than a month after David Grusch's July 2023 testimony, was to demand from the IC Inspector General the names of the people and the identities of the facilities involved in those programs. Its members subsequently drove the FY2024 NDAA's UAP Records Collection at the National Archives, the House Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, the September 2025 whistleblower hearing, and the UAP Disclosure Act amendment adopted into the House FY2027 NDAA on 22 July 2026 with its eminent domain provision intact — a provision that would order the government to seize recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence held by private entities. In August 2026 the relationship inverted: the executive branch authorised Burlison's House office to publish ODNI memo ES 2026-00818, making the oversight bloc the administration's distribution channel for its own IC directive.
entityDossier.narrative:
On 26 July 2023 the House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs held the first public UAP hearing to take testimony from military pilots and whistleblowers. David Grusch, a former intelligence officer, testified that he could not provide specific details regarding UAP crash retrieval or reverse engineering programs because those details are classified, but that he had provided them to the Office of the Inspector General of the Intelligence Community. Twenty-seven days later, on 22 August 2023, Tim Burchett announced that he had launched the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Caucus and had led five colleagues in a letter to IC IG Thomas A. Monheim asking for follow-up on Grusch's testimony — specifically, in the caucus's own words, "information from the Intelligence Community Inspector General regarding which people and facilities are involved with UAP crash retrieval programs and reverse engineering programs."

That question has never been publicly answered. The caucus's subsequent trajectory is best read as successive attempts to answer it by other means.

The statutory route came first. The FY2022 NDAA (Pub. L. 117-81, § 1683, codified at 50 U.S.C. § 3373) created AARO. The FY2023 NDAA (Pub. L. 117-263, § 1673, codified at 50 U.S.C. § 3373b) required a secure channel for authorised disclosure of UAP information relating to any government or contractor activity, notwithstanding NDAs, EO 13526, the Atomic Energy Act and Section 798 of the Espionage Act, and prohibited retaliation by agencies and by contractors, subcontractors, grantees and subgrantees. The FY2024 NDAA (Pub. L. 118-31, § 1841) then created the UAP Records Collection at the National Archives, defining covered records as any "Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence." That statutory phrase — "technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence" — is now U.S. public law, drafted by a Congress that would not have needed the category if nothing occupied it.

The FY2024 NDAA also contained the sharpest instrument the caucus era produced and the one that quietly died: sections 1687 and 7343 prohibited the use of FY2024 funds for any UAP-related secret program until the Secretary of Defense or the Director of National Intelligence fully disclosed the relevant details to the appropriate congressional committees and leadership. Those funding limitations were not renewed in subsequent enactments. Whoever allowed that lapse removed the only appropriations-side leverage Congress had ever applied to the question.

The Senate route was the UAP Disclosure Act, which passed the Senate in 2023 as Division G of S. 2226 by unanimous-consent incorporation of Amendment No. 935 and would have created an independent review board empowered to advise the President on declassification and release of UAP records. Its most aggressive clause orders the government to "exercise eminent domain over any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities in the interests of the public good." It was stripped in conference. On 22 July 2026 the House adopted its own version — including the eminent domain provision — as an amendment to the FY2027 NDAA, recorded as Amendment No. 315 at H.R. Rep. 119-755, pages 419-442. The named sponsors are Burlison of Missouri, Crane of Arizona, Carson of Indiana, Luna of Florida, Moskowitz of Florida and Begich of Alaska: three of the six are caucus founders, and Crane, Carson and Begich extend the coalition. The House bloc carried into law-adjacent text the provision the Senate had been unable to protect.

The hearing route continued through the 119th Congress. Luna chairs the Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, which held a hearing on 9 September 2025 titled "Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection," taking testimony from Air Force veteran Jeffrey Nuccetelli, Chief Alexandro Wiggins, journalist George Knapp and Air Force veteran Dylan Borland. That task force also runs the JFK files declassification work — the same members, the same theory of the case, applied to two record sets.

The most revealing development is procedural rather than legislative. On 21 July 2026 Burlison publicly invited anyone covered by President Trump's UAP NDA directive to contact his office for help navigating the process — a member of Congress standing up an informal whistleblower intake because the official one did not yet exist. Eleven days later, ODNI signed memorandum ES 2026-00818. On 1 August 2026 Burlison released it, noting that "the administration authorized Congressman Burlison's office to publicly distribute the memorandum." A national-level Intelligence Community directive to the Director of the CIA and the heads of every IC element reached the public through the website of a backbench House member from southwest Missouri who had spent three years accusing that same community of concealment. Whether that is co-option or capitulation is the open question; either way it is the clearest measure of the caucus's leverage in 2026. It is also worth noting what the memo Burlison distributed does not give him: it forecloses disclosure to Congress outside AARO, meaning the caucus published an instrument that routes around itself.

One cataloguing caution for downstream analysis: the domain uapcaucus.com belongs to a private advocacy organisation, not to the congressional caucus, and the House caucus has never published an official membership roster.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the U.S. civil space agency. Since 2022 it has been a formal participant in the government's UAP effort through a commissioned Independent Study Team, whose final report it published on 14 September 2023 alongside the appointment of a Director of UAP Research. Since 2026 it has been a contributing agency to the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters, supplying Apollo- and Gemini-era imagery and astronaut accounts.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: NASA's role in the concealment architecture is not custody; it is certification. It is the civilian, scientifically credentialed institution that repeatedly states there is no evidence of extraterrestrial origin while holding, by its own design choices, no access to the compartmented material where the question would actually be settled — its Independent Study Team used unclassified data only, and its charter expressly excluded review of past incidents. The sharper fact is a custody claim. In 2025 NASA's Office of Communications told a records researcher that it has no UAP records qualifying for transfer to the National Archives under the FY2024 NDAA because "any agency-related records associated with UAP, came from, and are owned by, the U.S. Department of Defense." That single sentence removes NASA's UAP holdings from the statutory records regime by attributing ownership to the department least likely to release them. Ten months later NASA's own Administrator publicly identified NASA-provided Apollo 12 and Apollo 17 lunar-surface imagery as "some of the most interesting data that NASA has provided as part of the UAP disclosure." Both statements cannot sit comfortably together: an agency with nothing to transfer, holding the most interesting data.
entityDossier.narrative:
NASA entered the modern UAP file formally in 2022, when it commissioned an outside Independent Study Team to advise on how the agency might contribute. The team's final report was published on 14 September 2023 under NASA release 23-106, chaired by David Spergel, president of the Simons Foundation, with sixteen members. Its overall recommendation was that NASA play a prominent role in the whole-of-government effort by using its open-source resources, technological expertise, data analysis techniques, federal and commercial partnerships, and Earth-observing assets to curate a better dataset for understanding future UAP. The report explicitly is not a review or assessment of previous UAP incidents. That boundary is the point: NASA's charter for the study excluded the historical record, which is where the legacy program question lives.

Spergel described the methodological constraint as a virtue: "Using unclassified data was essential for our team's fact-finding, open-communication collaboration, and for upholding scientific rigor to produce this report for NASA." The team reported that there are currently a limited number of high-quality observations of UAP, which make it impossible to draw firm scientific conclusions about their nature. The same architecture reappears three years later in the UAP Science Advisory Council chaired by Avi Loeb — unclassified data only, chartered to recommend how to get better data, structurally incapable of reaching a custody finding. NASA built the template.

With the report NASA named Mark McInerney its Director of UAP Research. McInerney had previously served as NASA's liaison to the Department of Defense "covering limited UAP activities for the agency" — meaning the agency's UAP function had already existed as a DoD liaison billet before it was given a public title. Administrator Bill Nelson framed the role in terms of instrumentation and analytics: the director would apply "artificial intelligence and machine learning to search the skies for anomalies," and "NASA will do this work transparently for the benefit of humanity." McInerney's career runs through NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, NOAA and the National Hurricane Center since 1996 — a NOAA lineage he shares with Tim Gallaudet, the retired admiral now on the 2026 UAP Science Advisory Council.

Then came the records question, and with it the most consequential NASA statement in the public record. The FY2024 NDAA, sections 1841-1842, required federal agencies to identify and transfer UAP records to a new collection at the National Archives, with digital transfers due by 30 September 2025. Record Group 615 was created to hold them. Over the course of 2025 the FAA, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the National Security Agency, ODNI and the Office of the Secretary of Defense transferred records into the online catalog. NASA did not. Asked why, NASA's Office of Communications replied: "Per the requirements in Section 1841-1842 of the Fiscal Year 2024 National Defense Authorization Act for handling records related to unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP), NASA does not have any records that meet the requirements to submit records to the National Archives. Any agency-related records associated with UAP, came from, and are owned by, the U.S. Department of Defense." That is not a denial of possession. It is an assertion of foreign ownership over material NASA holds — a jurisdictional argument that keeps agency UAP records outside a statutory public-release regime by routing their custody back into the Department of War.

The 2026 disclosure wave then produced the contradiction. On 27 May 2026, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman told Fox News Digital that the newly declassified files show "real unexplained phenomena" but no recovered craft: "What's being surfaced isn't crashed ships or alien bodies, but real unexplained phenomena," and "There's nothing I'm aware of in terms of alien bodies or spaceships." Note the construction — personal awareness, from a political appointee without read-in to the compartments where such material would be held. In the same interview Isaacman said agencies "really didn't take this quite as seriously in the past until President Trump put out the tweet, basically giving an order to government agencies and going out and saying, look, this time you better go through the files, you better start searching your databases and bring things up" — a sitting NASA Administrator stating that federal agencies did not conduct records searches for UAP material until a presidential post compelled them.

And on NASA's own contribution: "I would say that some of the most interesting data that NASA has provided as part of the UAP disclosure was taken on the surface of the moon from Apollo 12 and 17. You can't be a moon landing denier and also believe that those photos captured unexplained phenomenon." Fox News reported that the PURSUE material includes astronaut and NASA-related accounts from the Apollo and Gemini eras describing strange lights and unidentified objects observed in space, alongside 2023 infrared footage of an F-16 engaging a diamond-shaped object over Lake Huron and reports from military operations in Iran, Syria, Iraq and Greece. Set against the 2025 Office of Communications statement — NASA has no qualifying records because DoD owns them — the position is that NASA's most interesting UAP data was released through the Department of War's website rather than deposited in the National Archives collection Congress created for exactly that purpose. One route is statutory, permanent and indexed; the other is a rolling, discretionary web publication controlled by the Secretary of War. NASA's material went down the second.

A loose thread worth pulling: on the war.gov PURSUE page, the Release 05 slideshow of 7 August 2026 carries an image described as "A photograph of an unidentified object in low-Earth orbit, taken from Space Shuttle Columbia in 1996," while the underlying file is named DOW-UAP-D098_Film-Analysis-of-Unidentified-Objects_1953.jpg. A 1996 Columbia photograph filed under a 1953 film analysis is either a metadata error or an indexing artifact, and either way it is a checkable discrepancy in the government's own release. The Columbia 1996 imagery in question is almost certainly from STS-75, the tethered satellite mission whose downlink footage has been argued over for thirty years — meaning the 2026 disclosure has quietly placed a long-contested NASA video into an official unresolved-case release.

entityDossier.denialPosture: NASA's denial operates in three layers, each with an escape hatch. The 2023 Independent Study Team found no evidence of extraterrestrial origin while working exclusively from unclassified data and explicitly excluding past incidents from its charter. The 2025 Office of Communications statement denies possession of transferable records by asserting DoD ownership rather than absence — a custody argument, not a factual one. And Administrator Isaacman's 2026 formulation, 'There's nothing I'm aware of in terms of alien bodies or spaceships,' limits the denial to the personal knowledge of an appointee with no read-in to the compartments in question. Each is technically defensible and none touches the underlying question.
